brief: Kevin Warsh's FOMC speech addressed monetary policy's role in inflation but avoided assigning government (budget, trade, regulations, war) any responsibility, which kept post-speech concerns about the Fed-Treasury accord quiet but left the long end of the yield curve unmoved. Market probability of a hike at the next meeting sits at 68%, far below the ~95% certainty typical two weeks before a meeting, because softening data (ISM new orders, JOLTS quit rate, consumer confidence) leads inflation lower. Taylor Rule models using standard inputs imply a funds rate above 5% (range 4.47%-6.83%), but using the Dallas Fed's 6M trimmed-mean inflation (2.35%) instead puts the funds rate about where it already is, so no hike is needed. Rising 10-year yields reflect budget deficits, capex demand, and normalization after Fed suppression rather than US credit stress, since German, Japanese and UK yields moved similarly while only France and Italy spreads widened. The author expects Warsh to find room in August CPI, PPI, and employment data to hold rates through year-end, and still recommends cheap portfolio insurance given the added volatility risk.
